title: Pommes purée
subtitle: Robuchon-style butter-rich French mashed potato
excerpt: Silky, ultra-smooth mashed potato made with equal weights of potato and butter and pushed through a fine drum sieve. The French version of mash, served in small portions alongside grilled fish or roasted meat.
sourceNotes: Pommes purée in the style associated with Joël Robuchon, who refined it to its extreme form in his Paris restaurants from the 1980s. The method (equal parts potato and butter, sieved not mashed) is widely described in French culinary reference works including Paul Bocuse, La Cuisine du Marché and various Escoffier-tradition manuals in the public domain.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be made up to 1 hour ahead and kept warm in a heatproof bowl over a pan of barely simmering water, stirring occasionally.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sieve with a fine mesh stretched across a frame, used to push cooked potatoes or other vegetables through for an extremely smooth, lump-free texture.

content.text: Pommes purée is the French butter-rich version of mashed potato: smooth to the point of being almost liquid, served in a small mound or piped alongside meat or fish. The method is disciplined. Equal weights of potato and cold butter. A
instead of a masher. Warm milk, added slowly, to bring it to the right consistency.

The result is nothing like British mash. It is richer, smoother, and served in much smaller portions. A spoonful alongside a piece of pan-roasted salmon or a grilled fillet of sole is all it needs to be.

items.prepNote: floury variety, peeled and cut into even pieces

content.text: A drum sieve or a potato ricer is essential here. A masher will not give the right result. Have a warm bowl ready to receive the purée as you work.

Put {{potato}} of potato pieces in a large saucepan. Cover with cold, well-salted water. Bring to the boil and cook for 20 to 25 minutes until completely tender when pierced with a knife. Do not undercook: the potato must be soft all the way through.
Drain thoroughly. Return to the dry pan over low heat for 2 minutes, shaking, to drive off excess moisture. The drier the potato, the more butter and milk it can absorb.
Push the hot potato through a drum sieve or ricer into a warm, heavy-based saucepan. Set over low heat.

Beat in {{unsalted-butter}} of cold butter, a few cubes at a time, stirring vigorously with a wooden spoon or spatula. Add each new batch only when the previous one has been fully incorporated. The purée will look glossy and smooth.
Add the warm milk a little at a time, stirring, until the purée is the consistency you want: it should flow slowly off the spoon, not hold a stiff peak. Season well with salt. Taste and adjust.

items.cause: Not enough butter or milk added, or potato not dried enough before buttering
items.fix: Add more warm milk, a tablespoon at a time, until the texture loosens. Ensure the potato is bone-dry before you begin adding butter.

items.cause: Potato was overcooked until it began to disintegrate, or a waxy variety was used
items.fix: Use a floury potato variety. Cook until just tender, not beyond. Push through the sieve while still hot.

items.symptom: Purée tastes flat despite plenty of butter
items.fix: Salt the cooking water generously. Season the finished purée with flaky salt and taste again before serving.

items.symptom: Butter splits or the purée looks greasy
items.cause: Butter added too quickly, or the potato cooled too much before buttering began
items.fix: Always work with hot potato and cold butter. Add the butter in small pieces, not all at once. If it splits, a splash of warm milk and vigorous stirring can bring it back.

content.text: Pommes purée in this form is French restaurant cooking, not home cooking. Joël Robuchon's equal-weight method became famous through his Paris restaurants in the 1980s. It now appears on bistro menus worldwide. At home, half the weight of potato in butter still gives something far richer than ordinary mash, and is the right pairing for grilled fish, roast chicken, or beef.
